* In 1929, German [Paul Bauer](/wiki/Paul_Bauer_(mountaineer) "Paul Bauer (mountaineer)") led an expedition team that reached 7,400 m (24,300 ft) on the northeast spur before being turned back by a five-day [storm](/wiki/Storm "Storm").[[41]](#cite_note-Bauer-41)
* In May 1929, the American E. F. Farmer left Darjeeling with native porters, crossed the Kang La into Nepal and climbed up towards the *Talung Saddle*. When his porters refused to go any further, he climbed alone further upwards through drifting mists but did not return.[[17]](#cite_note-Smythe-17)
* In 1930, [Günter Dyhrenfurth](/wiki/G%C3%BCnter_Dyhrenfurth "Günter Dyhrenfurth") led an international expedition comprising the German Uli Wieland, [Austrian](/wiki/Austrians "Austrians") [Erwin Schneider](/wiki/Erwin_Schneider "Erwin Schneider") and [Englishman](/wiki/English_people "English people") [Frank Smythe](/wiki/Frank_Smythe "Frank Smythe") who attempted to climb Kangchenjunga. They failed because of poor weather and snow conditions.[[17]](#cite_note-Smythe-17)
* In 1931, Paul Bauer led a second German expedition team who attempted the northeast spur before being turned back by bad weather, illnesses and deaths. The team, including [Peter Aufschnaiter](/wiki/Peter_Aufschnaiter "Peter Aufschnaiter"), retreated after climbing 300 m higher than the 1929 attempt.[[41]](#cite_note-Bauer-41)
* In 1954, [John Kempe](/wiki/John_Kempe "John Kempe") led a party comprising John W. Tucker, S. R. Jackson, G. C. Lewis, [T. H. Braham](/wiki/Trevor_Braham "Trevor Braham") and medical officer Donald Stafford Matthews. They explored the upper Yalung glacier with the intention to discover a practicable route to the great ice-shelf that runs across the southwest face of Kangchenjunga.[[42]](#cite_note-42) This reconnaissance led to the route used by the successful 1955 expedition.[[43]](#cite_note-43)

**Telephone numbers in the People's Republic of China** are administered according to the Telecommunications Network Numbering Plan of China. The structure of [telephone numbers](/wiki/Telephone_number "Telephone number") for landlines and mobile service is different. Landline telephone numbers have area codes, whereas mobile numbers do not. In major cities, landline numbers consist of a two-digit area code followed by an eight-digit local number. In other places, landline numbers consist of a three-digit area code followed by a seven- or eight-digit local number. Mobile phone numbers consist of eleven digits.

Landline calls within the same area do not require the area code. Calls to other areas require dialing the trunk prefix *0* and the area code.

The [special administrative regions](/wiki/Special_administrative_regions_of_China "Special administrative regions of China") of [Hong Kong](/wiki/Hong_Kong "Hong Kong") and [Macau](/wiki/Macau "Macau") are not part of this numbering plan, and use the calling codes [852](/wiki/%2B852 "+852") and [853](/wiki/%2B853 "+853") respectively.

For many years, the origin of Cabernet Sauvignon was not clearly understood, and many myths and conjectures surrounded it. Until recently, the grape was rumoured to have ancient origins, perhaps even being the *Biturica* grape used to make [ancient Roman wine](/wiki/Ancient_Roman_wine "Ancient Roman wine") and referenced by [Pliny the Elder](/wiki/Pliny_the_Elder "Pliny the Elder"). This belief was widely held in the 18th century, when the grape was also known as *Petite Vidure* or *Bidure*, apparently a corruption of *Biturica*. There was also a belief that *Vidure* was a reference to the hardwood (French *vigne dure*) of the vine, with a possible relationship to [Carménère](/wiki/Carm%C3%A9n%C3%A8re "Carménère") which was once known as *Grand Vidure*.[[2]](#cite_note-Clarke_pg_47-56-2) Another theory was that the grapevine originated in the [Rioja](/wiki/La_Rioja_(Spain) "La Rioja (Spain)") region of [Spain](/wiki/Spain "Spain").[[3]](#cite_note-Goldstein_pg_134-139-3)

While the period when the name *Cabernet Sauvignon* became more prevalent over *Petite Vidure* is not certain, records indicate that the grape was a popular Bordeaux planting in the 18th century [Médoc](/wiki/M%C3%A9doc "Médoc") region.
